content: Accurate and rapid diagnostic tests for SARS-CoV-2 infection are essential tools for managing the COVID-19 pandemic. Rapid antigen tests, which can detect current infections, have the potential to improve access to testing, accelerate the detection of infections, and guide clinical and public health decisions to reduce viral transmission. This review evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of rapid, point-of-care antigen tests, with a focus on their performance in both symptomatic and asymptomatic populations. The review included studies that assessed the accuracy of commercially available rapid antigen tests. These studies involved individuals with suspected or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, those without infection, or those undergoing routine screening. The reference standard for determining infection status was primarily laboratory-based molecular testing, such as reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). The review analyzed data from 155 study cohorts, encompassing 100,462 unique samples, of which 16,822 were confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases. Most studies were conducted in Europe and evaluated 49 different commercial antigen tests. The sensitivity of the tests varied significantly across studies, while specificity was consistently high. In symptomatic individuals, the average sensitivity was 73.0% (95% CI: 69.3% to 76.4%), compared to 54.7% (95% CI: 47.7% to 61.6%) in asymptomatic individuals. Sensitivity was highest during the first week after symptom onset, reaching 80.9% (95% CI: 76.9% to 84.4%), but declined to 53.8% (95% CI: 48.0% to 59.6%) in the second week. Among asymptomatic individuals, sensitivity was higher when there was a suspected epidemiological exposure to SARS-CoV-2 (64.3%, 95% CI: 54.6% to 73.0%) compared to settings where testing was widely available (49.6%, 95% CI: 42.1% to 57.1%). Specificity was high across both symptomatic (99.1%) and asymptomatic (99.7%) groups. However, sensitivity decreased as viral load in the samples declined. The performance of antigen tests also varied by brand. When used according to manufacturer instructions, sensitivities ranged from 34.3% to 91.3% in symptomatic individuals and from 28.6% to 77.8% in asymptomatic individuals. Seven assays achieved sensitivities of 80% or higher in symptomatic individuals, meeting the World Health Organization (WHO) performance criteria. Specificity standards set by the WHO (≥97%) were met by 17 of 20 assays, with 12 achieving specificities above 99%. For asymptomatic individuals, only two assays approached but did not meet WHO sensitivity standards. At a 5% prevalence rate in symptomatic individuals during the first week of illness, the positive predictive value (PPV) was 89%, meaning that 1 in 10 positive results would be a false positive, and approximately 1 in 5 cases would be missed. At a 0.5% prevalence rate in asymptomatic individuals, the PPV ranged from 38% to 52%, indicating that 2 in 5 to 1 in 2 positive results would be false positives, and 1 in 2 to 1 in 3 cases would be missed. The authors concluded that the sensitivity of antigen tests varies widely. In symptomatic individuals, sensitivity is highest during the first week of illness when viral loads are higher. Tests that meet WHO performance standards could serve as alternatives to RT-PCR in situations requiring immediate clinical decisions or where RT-PCR is not readily available. However, antigen tests are better suited as a triage tool for RT-PCR testing. The lower sensitivity of antigen tests means that negative results do not rule out infection. While evidence for testing in asymptomatic populations has increased, sensitivity remains lower, and there is limited data on their use in diverse settings. Further research is needed to assess the effectiveness of antigen test-based screening programs in reducing transmission, including in schools, healthcare settings, and among travelers.
